prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a complaint about a slow claim. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a claim is dragging on because we are waiting on a third party, I should say plainly what is outstanding, who is holding it up, and the next review date so the member can see progress even if the file is not yet settled."},{"type":"fact","content":"When I cannot complete a decision within delegated authority, I should explain that escalation is part of the process rather than leaving the member to guess why the case has gone quiet."},{"type":"preference","content":"When a member is frustrated about delay, I should acknowledge the inconvenience first and keep the update brief and practical, because a long explanation usually feels like more stalling."},{"type":"observation","content":"When key evidence is missing, I should ask for it in one clear list instead of sending several small requests, as repeated chases can make a slow claim feel even slower."},{"type":"fact","content":"When repairs, engineer reports, or cover checks are awaited, I should note the expected turnaround and set a reminder to chase before the member has to do it."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a complaint about delay comes in, it often means the member wants certainty more than speed, so I should confirm what can be paid now, what cannot, and why."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I am updating a case after a quiet spell, I should lead with what has changed since the last contact, because members measure progress by movement rather than process detail."},{"type":"fact","content":"When there is an internal hand-off between claims teams, I should make the handover visible on the file and in the member update so the claim does not appear to have been forgotten."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a claim is simple but has become slow, I should check for avoidable blockers such as incorrect contact details, missing authority, or an unreviewed diary task before assuming the case is inherently complex."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I apologise for delay, I should pair it with a concrete next step and a timescale, because reassurance without action does not reduce complaint risk."}]}
